claim: Approximately 14,000 progeny were generated from crosses among 16 diverse yeast strains.
source: We generated ~14,000 progeny from crosses among 16 diverse yeast strains and identified thousands of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for 38 traits.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of progeny generated and the number of parental strains used.

claim: Thousands of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) were identified for 38 traits.
source: We generated ~14,000 progeny from crosses among 16 diverse yeast strains and identified thousands of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for 38 traits.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of QTLs and traits analyzed.

claim: Rare variants make a disproportionate contribution to trait variation.
source: We combined our results with sequencing data for 1011 yeast isolates to show that rare variants make a disproportionate contribution to trait variation.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from the segregant panel combined with population sequencing data to demonstrate this relationship.

claim: The disproportionate contribution of rare variants is driven by rare variants that arose recently.
source: Evolutionary analyses revealed that this contribution is driven by rare variants that arose recently, and that negative selection has shaped the relationship between variant frequency and effect size.
evidence: The manuscript uses evolutionary analyses comparing variants to S. paradoxus to determine ancestral state and timing.

claim: Negative selection has shaped the relationship between variant frequency and effect size.
source: Evolutionary analyses revealed that this contribution is driven by rare variants that arose recently, and that negative selection has shaped the relationship between variant frequency and effect size.
evidence: The manuscript presents evolutionary analyses and theoretical expectations about selection.

claim: Hundreds of QTLs were resolved to single genes.
source: We leveraged the structure of the crosses to resolve hundreds of QTLs to single genes.
evidence: The manuscript describes statistical fine-mapping results that identify causal genes.

claim: The 16 parental strains contain both alleles at 82% of biallelic SNPs and small indels observed at minor allele frequency >5% in a collection of 1011 S. cerevisiae strains.
source: Specifically, they contain both alleles at 82% of biallelic SNPs and small indels observed at minor allele frequency >5% in a collection of 1011 S. cerevisiae strains (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites comparison with the Peter et al. 2018 dataset to quantify genetic diversity captured.

claim: The panel of segregants consists of 13,950 individual recombinant haploid yeast segregants.
source: We constructed a panel of 13,950 individual recombinant haploid yeast segregants by crossing each parental strain to two different strains and collecting an average of 872 progeny per cross (Figure 1; Figure 1—source data 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of segregants constructed.

claim: Each parental strain was crossed to two different strains.
source: We constructed a panel of 13,950 individual recombinant haploid yeast segregants by crossing each parental strain to two different strains and collecting an average of 872 progeny per cross (Figure 1; Figure 1—source data 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the crossing design used.

claim: An average of 872 progeny per cross were collected.
source: We constructed a panel of 13,950 individual recombinant haploid yeast segregants by crossing each parental strain to two different strains and collecting an average of 872 progeny per cross (Figure 1; Figure 1—source data 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the average number of progeny per cross.

claim: Segregants were genotyped by highly multiplexed whole-genome sequencing with median 2.3-fold coverage per base per individual.
source: We genotyped these segregants by highly multiplexed whole-genome sequencing, with median 2.3-fold coverage per base per individual.
evidence: The manuscript describes the genotyping method and coverage achieved.

claim: Genotypes were called at 298,979 genetic variants.
source: Genotypes were called at 298,979 genetic variants, with an average of 71,117 genetic variants segregating in a single cross.
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of variants genotyped.

claim: An average of 71,117 genetic variants segregate in a single cross.
source: Genotypes were called at 298,979 genetic variants, with an average of 71,117 genetic variants segregating in a single cross.
evidence: The manuscript reports the average number of segregating variants per cross.

claim: Growth measurements in different environments are not strongly correlated.
source: Because the growth measurements in different environments are not strongly correlated, we treat them as separate phenotypes or traits (Bloom et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and cites a previous study.

claim: Additive genetic effects accounted for just over half of the total phenotypic variance on average.
source: We used a variance components model (Bloom et al., 2015; de los Campos et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2010) to show that, on average, additive genetic effects accounted for just over half of the total phenotypic variance, while pairwise genetic interactions accounted for 8%, approximately 1/6 as much as additive effects (Figure 2 inset; Supplementary file 2; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports variance component analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pairwise genetic interactions accounted for 8% of total phenotypic variance, approximately 1/6 as much as additive effects.
source: We used a variance components model (Bloom et al., 2015; de los Campos et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2010) to show that, on average, additive genetic effects accounted for just over half of the total phenotypic variance, while pairwise genetic interactions accounted for 8%, approximately 1/6 as much as additive effects (Figure 2 inset; Supplementary file 2; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports variance component analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claim: 4552 QTLs were mapped at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%.
source: We mapped 4552 QTLs at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%, with an average of 120 (range 52–195) QTLs per trait (Supplementary file 3; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of QTLs detected at a specified FDR threshold.

claim: An average of 120 QTLs per trait were detected, with a range of 52–195.
source: We mapped 4552 QTLs at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%, with an average of 120 (range 52–195) QTLs per trait (Supplementary file 3; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the average and range of QTLs per trait.

claim: The detected QTLs explain a median of 73% of the additive heritability per trait and cross.
source: The detected QTLs explain a median of 73% of the additive heritability per trait and cross, showing that we can account for most of the genetic contribution to trait variation with specific loci (Figure 2; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports cross-validation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within-cross QTL mapping found a median of 12 QTLs per trait at FDR of 5%.
source: We complemented the joint analysis with QTL mapping within each cross and found a median of 12 QTLs per trait at the same FDR of 5%.
evidence: The manuscript reports results from within-cross mapping analysis.

claim: Within-cross detected loci explained a median of 68% of the additive heritability.
source: The detected loci explained a median of 68% of the additive heritability (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the variance explained by within-cross mapping.

claim: The joint analysis was more powerful than within-cross analysis, explaining an additional 5% of trait variance.
source: The joint analysis was more powerful, explaining an additional 5% of trait variance and uncovering 458 QTLs not detected within individual crosses.
evidence: The manuscript compares the performance of joint versus within-cross analyses.

claim: The joint analysis uncovered 458 QTLs not detected within individual crosses.
source: The joint analysis was more powerful, explaining an additional 5% of trait variance and uncovering 458 QTLs not detected within individual crosses.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of additional QTLs detected by joint analysis.

claim: Additional QTLs detected by joint analysis had smaller effect sizes than those detected within crosses (median of 0.071 SD units vs 0.083 SD units).
source: Consistent with the higher statistical power of the joint analysis, these additional QTLs had smaller effect sizes (median of 0.071 SD units vs 0.083 SD units; Wilcoxon rank sum test W = 1e6, p=9e-5).
evidence: The manuscript reports effect size comparison with statistical test results.

claim: 27.8% of biallelic variants in the study were rare (MAF <0.01).
source: By this definition, 27.8% of biallelic variants in our study were rare.
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of rare variants based on the defined threshold.

claim: Across all traits, the median contribution of rare variants was 51.7%.
source: Across all traits, the median contribution of rare variants was 51.7%, despite the fact that they constituted only 27.8% of all variants and that a rare variant is expected to explain less variance than a common one with the same allelic effect size.
evidence: The manuscript reports variance partitioning results across traits.

claim: Rare variants are expected to explain less variance than common variants with the same allelic effect size.
source: Across all traits, the median contribution of rare variants was 51.7%, despite the fact that they constituted only 27.8% of all variants and that a rare variant is expected to explain less variance than a common one with the same allelic effect size.
evidence: This is a statement of statistical expectation based on allele frequency.

claim: Growth in the presence of copper sulfate and lithium chloride showed almost no contribution from rare variants.
source: Comparing different traits, we saw a wide range of the relative contribution of rare variants, from almost none for growth in the presence of copper sulfate and lithium chloride to over 75% for growth in the presence of cadmium chloride, in low pH, at high temperature, and on minimal medium (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports trait-specific variance partitioning results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Growth in the presence of cadmium chloride, in low pH, at high temperature, and on minimal medium showed over 75% contribution from rare variants.
source: Comparing different traits, we saw a wide range of the relative contribution of rare variants, from almost none for growth in the presence of copper sulfate and lithium chloride to over 75% for growth in the presence of cadmium chloride, in low pH, at high temperature, and on minimal medium (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports trait-specific variance partitioning results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Copper sulfate and lithium chloride traits had the most phenotypic variance explained by detected GWAS loci in the 1011 sequenced yeast strains.
source: The results for copper sulfate and lithium chloride are consistent with GWAS for these traits in the 1011 sequenced yeast strains—these two traits had the most phenotypic variance explained by detected GWAS loci, which inherently correspond to common variants, with large contributions coming from known common copy-number variation at the CUP and ENA loci, respectively (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites GWAS results from Peter et al. 2018 to support the findings.

claim: Large contributions to copper sulfate and lithium chloride trait variation come from known common copy-number variation at the CUP and ENA loci, respectively.
source: The results for copper sulfate and lithium chloride are consistent with GWAS for these traits in the 1011 sequenced yeast strains—these two traits had the most phenotypic variance explained by detected GWAS loci, which inherently correspond to common variants, with large contributions coming from known common copy-number variation at the CUP and ENA loci, respectively (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites known genetic architecture from Peter et al. 2018.

claim: Most QTLs had small effects (64% of QTLs had effects less than 0.1 SD units).
source: Most QTLs had small effects (64% of QTLs had effects less than 0.1 SD units) and most lead variants were common (78%), consistent with previous linkage and association studies.
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of QTL effect sizes.

claim: Most lead variants were common (78%).
source: Most QTLs had small effects (64% of QTLs had effects less than 0.1 SD units) and most lead variants were common (78%), consistent with previous linkage and association studies.
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency distribution of lead variants.

claim: QTLs with large effects were highly enriched for rare variants.
source: We observed that QTLs with large effects were highly enriched for rare variants, and conversely, that rare variants were highly enriched for large effect sizes (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the relationship between effect size and allele frequency shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rare variants were highly enriched for large effect sizes.
source: We observed that QTLs with large effects were highly enriched for rare variants, and conversely, that rare variants were highly enriched for large effect sizes (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports the relationship between effect size and allele frequency shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Among QTLs with an absolute effect of at least 0.3 SD units, 145 of the corresponding lead variants were rare and only 90 were common.
source: For instance, among QTLs with an absolute effect of at least 0.3 SD units, 145 of the corresponding lead variants were rare and only 90 were common.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific counts of rare versus common variants among large-effect QTLs.

claim: Rare variants were 6.7 times more likely to have an effect greater than 0.3 SD.
source: Rare variants were 6.7 times more likely to have an effect greater than 0.3 SD (Figure 3—source data 1, Fisher's exact test, p<2e-16).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment analysis with statistical test results.

claim: For traits under negative selection, variant effect size is expected to be a decreasing function of minor allele frequency.
source: Theoretical population genetics models show that for traits under negative selection, variant effect size is expected to be a decreasing function of minor allele frequency (Eyre-Walker, 2010; Pritchard, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical population genetics models.

claim: The empirically observed relationship between effect size and allele frequency provides evidence that most traits examined have evolved under negative selection in the yeast population.
source: We empirically observe this relationship in our data for most of the traits examined, providing evidence that they have evolved under negative selection in the yeast population (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the observed data in light of theoretical expectations about selection.

claim: Recently arising deleterious alleles have had less time to be purged by negative selection.
source: Recently arising deleterious alleles have had less time to be purged by negative selection, and therefore recent variants are expected to have stronger effects on gene function, and hence manifest as QTLs with larger effects.
evidence: The manuscript presents a theoretical expectation based on population genetics principles.

claim: Recent variants are expected to have stronger effects on gene function than ancient variants.
source: Recently arising deleterious alleles have had less time to be purged by negative selection, and therefore recent variants are expected to have stronger effects on gene function, and hence manifest as QTLs with larger effects.
evidence: The manuscript presents a theoretical expectation based on population genetics principles.

claim: Recent variants were 1.8 times more likely than ancient variants to have an effect size greater than 0.1 SD units.
source: Consistent with this expectation, we observed that recent variants were 1.8 times more likely than ancient variants to have an effect size greater than 0.1 SD units (Fisher's exact test p=9e-5) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment analysis comparing recent and ancient variants with statistical test results.

claim: Recent variants were 1.5 times more likely to decrease fitness.
source: We further examined the direction of QTL effects and found that recent variants were 1.5 times more likely to decrease fitness (Fisher's exact test p=8e-3).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of effect direction with statistical test results.

claim: No ancient variant decreased fitness by more than 0.5 SD units, whereas 41 recent variants did.
source: Strikingly, no ancient variant decreased fitness by more than 0.5 SD units, whereas 41 recent variants did (Fisher's exact test p=7e-3).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific counts of large-effect deleterious variants by ancestral state with statistical test results.

claim: 427 QTLs were resolved to single causal genes at an FDR of 20%.
source: With this approach, we resolved 427 QTLs to single causal genes at an FDR of 20%.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical fine-mapping results.

claim: The 427 resolved QTLs contain 195 unique genes.
source: Because some QTLs have pleiotropic effects on multiple traits, this gene set contains 195 unique genes, greatly expanding the repertoire of causal genes in yeast.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of unique causal genes identified.

claim: 26 of the 195 genes identified are supported by previous experimental evidence as causal for yeast trait variation.
source: We searched the literature and found that 26 of the 195 genes identified here are supported by previous experimental evidence as causal for yeast trait variation (Fay, 2013; Jerison et al., 2017; Sadhu et al., 2016; Treusch et al., 2015; Wang and Kruglyak, 2014) (Figure 4B; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of identified genes against prior experimental studies.

claim: At a more stringent FDR of 5%, 105 unique causal genes were found, which included 24 of the 26 genes with experimental evidence.
source: At a more stringent FDR of 5%, we found 105 unique causal genes, which included 24 of the 26 genes with experimental evidence.
evidence: The manuscript reports fine-mapping results at a more stringent threshold.

claim: Causal genes were highly enriched for GO terms related to the plasma membrane (45 of 522, 16.5 expected, q = 1.8e-7).
source: Causal genes were highly enriched for GO terms related to the plasma membrane (45 of 522, 16.5 expected, q = 1.8e-7), metal ion transport (13 of 83, 2.6 expected, q = 0.0009), and positive regulation of nitrogen compound biosynthesis (28 of 393, 12.5 expected, q = 0.0076) (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results with statistical significance.

claim: Causal genes were highly enriched for GO terms related to metal ion transport (13 of 83, 2.6 expected, q = 0.0009).
source: Causal genes were highly enriched for GO terms related to the plasma membrane (45 of 522, 16.5 expected, q = 1.8e-7), metal ion transport (13 of 83, 2.6 expected, q = 0.0009), and positive regulation of nitrogen compound biosynthesis (28 of 393, 12.5 expected, q = 0.0076) (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results with statistical significance.

claim: Causal genes were highly enriched for GO terms related to positive regulation of nitrogen compound biosynthesis (28 of 393, 12.5 expected, q = 0.0076).
source: Causal genes were highly enriched for GO terms related to the plasma membrane (45 of 522, 16.5 expected, q = 1.8e-7), metal ion transport (13 of 83, 2.6 expected, q = 0.0009), and positive regulation of nitrogen compound biosynthesis (28 of 393, 12.5 expected, q = 0.0076) (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports GO enrichment analysis results with statistical significance.

claim: Five of the six genes involved in cAMP biosynthesis were identified as causal (IRA1, IRA2, BCY1, CYR1, and RAS1; 0.19 expected, q = 0.0002).
source: Strikingly, five of the six genes involved in cAMP biosynthesis were identified as causal (IRA1, IRA2, BCY1, CYR1, and RAS1; 0.19 expected, q = 0.0002).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment of specific pathway genes with statistical significance.

claim: Additional genes in the RAS/cAMP signaling pathway were identified as causal, including GPR1, SRV2, and RHO3.
source: Additional genes in the RAS/cAMP signaling pathway were also identified as causal, including GPR1, which is involved in glucose sensing, SRV2, which binds adenylate cyclase, and RHO3, which encodes a RAS-like GTPase.
evidence: The manuscript reports additional causal genes in the pathway.

claim: In yeast, the RAS/cAMP pathway regulates cell cycle progression, metabolism, and stress resistance.
source: In yeast, the RAS/cAMP pathway regulates cell cycle progression, metabolism, and stress resistance (Tisi et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about the RAS/cAMP pathway.

claim: Variation in many RAS/cAMP pathway genes influenced growth on alternative carbon sources.
source: Variation in many of these genes influenced growth on alternative carbon sources.
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic effects of variation in pathway genes.

claim: The yeast population contains abundant functional variation in genes that regulate the switch from glucose to alternative carbon sources through the RAS/cAMP pathway.
source: We hypothesize that the yeast population contains abundant functional variation in genes that regulate the switch from glucose to alternative carbon sources through the RAS/cAMP pathway.
evidence: The manuscript presents a hypothesis based on the observed data.

claim: The majority of heritable phenotypic differences arise from additive genetic effects in yeast crosses.
source: We previously used a cross between lab (BY) and vineyard (RM) strains of yeast to show that the majority of heritable phenotypic differences arise from additive genetic effects, and we were able to detect, at genome-wide significance, specific loci that together account for the majority of quantitative trait variation (Bloom et al., 2015; Bloom et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work demonstrating this finding.

claim: The BY lab reference strain (S288c) is not exceptional from the standpoint of genetic variation and quantitative traits compared to other yeast isolates.
source: Our results here, obtained from crosses among 16 diverse strains, generalize these findings to the S. cerevisiae population and show that S288c is not exceptional from the standpoint of genetic variation and quantitative traits.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the current results in the context of previous concerns about S288c.

claim: The findings that the majority of genetic variance of most traits is additive will apply broadly beyond yeast.
source: We believe that the findings that the majority of the genetic variance of most traits is additive, and that there is little additive 'missing heritability' in studies with sufficiently large sample sizes, will apply broadly beyond yeast.
evidence: The manuscript presents a belief about the generalizability of findings.

claim: There is little additive 'missing heritability' in studies with sufficiently large sample sizes.
source: We believe that the findings that the majority of the genetic variance of most traits is additive, and that there is little additive 'missing heritability' in studies with sufficiently large sample sizes, will apply broadly beyond yeast.
evidence: The manuscript presents a belief based on the current findings.

claim: The detected QTLs likely capture the majority of common variants that segregate in S. cerevisiae and have appreciable phenotypic effects on growth.
source: These loci likely capture the majority of common variants that segregate in S. cerevisiae and have appreciable phenotypic effects on growth, and therefore provide a comprehensive starting point for more fine-grained analyses of the genetic contribution to quantitative trait variation.
evidence: The manuscript makes an inference about the comprehensiveness of the detected QTLs.

claim: Approximately 8% of the QTLs were localized to single genes based on genetic mapping information alone.
source: We were able to localize approximately 8% of the QTLs to single genes based on genetic mapping information alone.
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of QTLs fine-mapped to single genes.

claim: Different strains of S. cerevisiae may have evolved different strategies for nutrient sensing and response as a function of specializing in particular environmental niches.
source: Interestingly, these genes cluster in specific functional categories and pathways, suggesting that different strains of S. cerevisiae may have evolved different strategies for nutrient sensing and response as a function of specializing in particular environmental niches (Chantranupong et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript presents a hypothesis based on the functional clustering of causal genes.

claim: GWAS by design only test common DNA sequence variants.
source: GWAS by design only test common DNA sequence variants; however, recent studies underscore the likely importance of the contribution of rare variants to heritable variation (Wainschtein et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript states a known limitation of GWAS methodology.

claim: Recent studies underscore the likely importance of the contribution of rare variants to heritable variation.
source: GWAS by design only test common DNA sequence variants; however, recent studies underscore the likely importance of the contribution of rare variants to heritable variation (Wainschtein et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies on rare variant contributions.

claim: Purifying selection against variants that negatively affect fitness is expected to keep them at low frequencies in a population.
source: In particular, purifying selection against variants that negatively affect fitness is expected to keep them at low frequencies in a population, resulting in a predicted inverse relationship between effect sizes and allele frequencies for variants that influence fitness-related traits (Gibson, 2012; Goldstein et al., 2013; Kryukov et al., 2007; Pritchard, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical expectations from population genetics.

claim: An inverse relationship between effect sizes and allele frequencies is predicted for variants that influence fitness-related traits.
source: In particular, purifying selection against variants that negatively affect fitness is expected to keep them at low frequencies in a population, resulting in a predicted inverse relationship between effect sizes and allele frequencies for variants that influence fitness-related traits (Gibson, 2012; Goldstein et al., 2013; Kryukov et al., 2007; Pritchard, 2001).
evidence: The manuscript cites theoretical expectations from population genetics.

claim: An increased burden of ultra-rare protein-truncating variants has been observed in human diseases.
source: An increased burden of ultra-rare protein-truncating variants has been observed in human diseases (Ganna et al., 2018; Exome Aggregation Consortium et al., 2016), and multiple studies have found that GWAS variants with lower allele frequencies have larger effect sizes (Marouli et al., 2017; Park et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites empirical findings from human genetics studies.

claim: Multiple studies have found that GWAS variants with lower allele frequencies have larger effect sizes.
source: An increased burden of ultra-rare protein-truncating variants has been observed in human diseases (Ganna et al., 2018; Exome Aggregation Consortium et al., 2016), and multiple studies have found that GWAS variants with lower allele frequencies have larger effect sizes (Marouli et al., 2017; Park et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites empirical findings from GWAS studies.

claim: A negative correlation between allele frequency and effect size has been observed in maize GWAS.
source: A negative correlation between allele frequency and effect size has also been observed in maize GWAS (Wallace et al., 2014), and our previous work in yeast suggested that variants that contribute to trait variation are shifted to lower frequencies when compared to all sequence variants (Ehrenreich et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites empirical findings from maize genetics.

claim: Previous work in yeast suggested that variants that contribute to trait variation are shifted to lower frequencies when compared to all sequence variants.
source: A negative correlation between allele frequency and effect size has also been observed in maize GWAS (Wallace et al., 2014), and our previous work in yeast suggested that variants that contribute to trait variation are shifted to lower frequencies when compared to all sequence variants (Ehrenreich et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous findings from yeast genetics.

claim: Recent studies employed indirect variance partitioning approaches to uncover appreciable contributions of lower frequency variants to heritability of complex traits in humans.
source: Recent studies employed indirect variance partitioning approaches to uncover appreciable contributions of lower frequency variants to heritability of complex traits in humans, including prostate cancer susceptibility (Mancuso et al., 2016), height (Wainschtein et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2015), and body mass index (Wainschtein et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent human genetics studies using variance partitioning.

claim: Rare variants cannot be detected by GWAS by design.
source: First, rare variants cannot be detected by GWAS by design, and sequencing studies have not reached sufficient sample sizes to find them with high statistical power (Zuk et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript states a known limitation of GWAS methodology.

claim: Sequencing studies have not reached sufficient sample sizes to find rare variants with high statistical power.
source: First, rare variants cannot be detected by GWAS by design, and sequencing studies have not reached sufficient sample sizes to find them with high statistical power (Zuk et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study discussing power limitations in sequencing studies.

claim: The power to detect a variant with any given effect size decreases with the frequency of the variant in the study.
source: Second, the power to detect a variant with any given effect size decreases with the frequency of the variant in the study, simply because fewer individuals in the sample carry a less-frequent variant (Zuk et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study explaining statistical power considerations.

claim: The statistical artifact of decreased power for rare variants shifts the effect sizes of detected rare variants upwards, confounding effect size and allele frequency.
source: This statistical artifact shifts the effect sizes of those rare variants that are detected upwards, confounding effect size and allele frequency and biasing any effort to measure the underlying relationship between the two.
evidence: The manuscript explains a statistical bias in detecting rare variants.

claim: Variants that are rare in the yeast population and occur in only a single parental strain are present in approximately 1000 progeny in the mapping population.
source: In this mapping population, even variants that are rare in the yeast population and occur in only a single parental strain are present in approximately 1000 progeny, resulting in high power to detect them.
evidence: The manuscript explains the design advantage of the crossing scheme.

claim: The crossing design results in high power to detect rare variants.
source: In this mapping population, even variants that are rare in the yeast population and occur in only a single parental strain are present in approximately 1000 progeny, resulting in high power to detect them.
evidence: The manuscript explains the design advantage of the crossing scheme.

claim: The study decoupled variant frequency from effect size by measuring population allele frequencies in a separate large catalog of sequenced yeast isolates.
source: We then decoupled variant frequency from effect size by measuring the population allele frequencies of QTL lead variants detected in our panel in a separate large catalog of sequenced yeast isolates (Peter et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological approach to avoid confounding.
